prime.problem: At batch 1 an H100 does 0.12 µs of math in a 35 µs step on one Llama MLP matrix: 0.3% of the chip you're paying for. You need to know how many tokens a step must carry before the linear layers stop waiting on memory, and what changes that number.
prime.fits: Fourth card. It applies the roofline's matmul intensity ≈ B to every linear layer of a Transformer, names the threshold B<sub>crit</sub>, and adds the precision factor β. The attention card and the step-time card both lean on it.
expect: β: bits per weight ÷ bits per activation
batch means tokens per step, per replica
prime.goal: Derive B<sub>crit</sub> from the matmul bytes, compute it for a chip and a precision, and explain why decode rarely reaches it even though prefill always does.

attend: Which term of 2BD + 2DF + 2BF dominates in decode, and why does that make intensity equal to B?
Why is batch counted in tokens per replica rather than in sequences, and what does that mean for prefill?
Why do int8 weights with bf16 math halve B<sub>crit</sub>, while int8 × int8 leaves it unchanged?
Why doesn't a bigger GPU (H100 → B200) fix batch-1 utilisation?
If B<sub>crit</sub> is only about 300, what stops a decode server from simply running 300 users?

must: Each weight matrix is read once per step whatever B is → bytes ≈ 2DF while FLOPs = 2BDF → intensity ≈ B → the layer is compute-bound iff B > C/W<sub>hbm</sub> = B<sub>crit</sub> (240 v5e, 295 H100)

Below B<sub>crit</sub> extra tokens ride on the same weight read → step time barely moves (35.1 → 38.6 µs from B = 1 to 325 on one Llama MLP matrix) → throughput rises almost free; past it each token costs its own FLOPs → throughput stops improving while latency rises

Narrower weights with the same math precision cut bytes but not FLOPs → B<sub>crit</sub> scales by β (int8/fp8 weights + bf16 math → ½: 120 v5e, ≈ 148 H100) → faster narrow math alone doubles the ridge (591) → doing both cancels

Prefill puts every prompt token in one step → a 1,000-token prompt is B = 1,000 > 295 → always compute-bound; decode gets one token per sequence → needs ~300 concurrent sequences → each needs its own KV cache → HBM usually runs out first
elevated: MoE reads E experts' weights but each token only does k experts' FLOPs → B<sub>crit</sub> × E/k → 1,920 tokens for E = 16, k = 2 on v5e
reference: the Llama MLP utilisation table (0.3% at B = 1 … 100% at 512)
exact crossings 325.4 (H100) and 259.8 (v5e) with full bytes
the book's two H100 figures, about 280 and 295

compress.prompt: Derive B<sub>crit</sub> from scratch in four lines: FLOPs, bytes, the approximation, the inequality. Then write one line each for how int8 weights, fp8 × fp8 and MoE change it, and one line on why decode struggles to reach it.
checklist: FLOPs 2BDF, bytes 2BD + 2DF + 2BF ≈ 2DF when B ≪ D, F
intensity ≈ B, so compute-bound iff B > C/W
weight-only int8/fp8 halves it; narrow math on narrow weights leaves it
decode needs ~300 sequences, each with a KV cache, so memory caps the batch first

retrieve.q: Explain why B<sub>crit</sub> depends only on the chip and the precision, not on the model's width D or F (to first order).
answer: D and F appear in both FLOPs (2BDF) and bytes (≈ 2DF), so they cancel
what's left is B against the chip's FLOPs per byte
they come back only in the exact-bytes correction, which pushes the crossover up for small matrices (≈ 697 at D = F = 1024 on H100)

retrieve.q: Walk the B = 1 row for bf16[1, 4096] × bf16[4096, 14336] on an H100: bytes, FLOPs, both times and the utilisation.

A team switches from bf16 to fp8 matmuls on H100 with bf16 weights still in memory, expecting the decode step to speed up. What happens to B<sub>crit</sub> and to the batch-1 step, and what should they have done?
answer: faster math on the same bytes doubles the ridge to ≈ 591
batch-1 decode is bound by reading the weights, so the step doesn't change
quantize the weights too (fp8 × fp8): bytes halve, the step halves, and B<sub>crit</sub> returns to ≈ 295; weight-only fp8 lowers it to ≈ 148

compare.q: Linear layers have a B<sub>crit</sub>; decode attention has none. What is fundamentally different, and what lever works on attention instead?
answer: linear layers share one weight matrix across all tokens in the step; attention reads a separate KV cache per sequence
so batching raises linear intensity toward B<sub>crit</sub> but leaves attention near 1 (or G with GQA)
for attention the lever is fewer KV bytes (GQA, FP8 KV, paging), not a bigger batch

compare.q: For a mixture of experts, B<sub>crit</sub> multiplies by E/k. Which design choice of MoE causes that, and what does it mean for how many users an MoE server needs before its FLOPs stop idling?
answer: each token uses only k of E experts, so FLOPs scale with k while weight bytes read at large batch scale with E
the reuse per weight byte drops by E/k, so the batch must grow by E/k (1,920 on v5e for E = 16, k = 2; 3,840 for DeepSeek's 256/8 with int8 weights)
an MoE server needs far more concurrent tokens, which is why expert parallelism and large deployments go with MoE

predict.q: Move Llama-3.1-8B to an H200 (141 GB, 4.8 TB/s, 9.9e14 bf16 FLOP/s) at 2k context. Commit: what is B<sub>crit</sub> for bf16, how many 2k sequences fit, and does decode finally reach compute-bound on the MLP?
predict.answer: B<sub>crit</sub> = 9.9e14 / 4.8e12 ≈ 206, lower than H100's 295 because bandwidth grew and FLOPs didn't. Free HBM 141 − 16.06 = 124.9 GB fits ⌊124.9 / 0.268⌋ = 465 sequences of 2k. 465 > 206, so yes: the step-time card shows the MLP math (7.55 ms) overtaking the weight read (3.35 ms) at that batch.

apply.task: Recompute the card's worked matrix (bf16[B, 4096] × bf16[4096, 14336]) for an H200 at B = 64 using exact bytes: FLOPs, bytes, T<sub>math</sub>, T<sub>comms</sub> and utilisation. Then fill the β table's first two rows for the H200 (bf16 × bf16, and int8/fp8 weights with bf16 math).
apply.done: You get T<sub>math</sub> ≈ 7.6 µs, T<sub>comms</sub> ≈ 25.0 µs, utilisation ≈ 30% (memory-bound), and B<sub>crit</sub> ≈ 206 and ≈ 103 for the two rows.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the H200's B<sub>crit</sub>, or whether it reaches it?
Can you explain why more bandwidth lowers Bcrit, without saying the ratio changed?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: weight precision → β, or batch in tokens → prefill always compute-bound?
Could you say why decode's limit is memory capacity rather than B<sub>crit</sub> on one H100?
What will you check on the attention card: why attention gets no B<sub>crit</sub> at all?
